title: Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe: Opinion and Order Adopting Predictive-Coding Rulings
author: Andrew L. Carter Jr.

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency

Carter’s approval rests on deferential review, quality-assurance testing, party participation and the ability to revisit reliability—not proof of comparative superiority.

mo.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment

kp.k: Court upheld case-specific predictive coding under deferential review
kp.d: In the order dated April 25, 2012 and filed April 26, District Judge Andrew L. Carter Jr. adopted Magistrate Judge Andrew J. Peck’s discovery rulings and denied plaintiffs’ objections. The decision upheld predictive coding as specified in this case’s electronically stored information (ESI) protocol under Rule 72(a)’s clearly-erroneous-or-contrary-to-law standard; it did not establish general empirical superiority over keyword searching.
qs: Mindful of this highly deferential standard of review, the Court adopts Judge Peck’s rulings because they are well reasoned and they consider the potential advantages and pitfalls of the predictive coding software.
concluded that under the circumstances of this particular case, the use of the predictive coding software as specified in the ESI protocol is more appropriate than keyword searching.
The Court does not find a basis to hold that his conclusion is clearly erroneous or contrary to law.

kp.k: Reliability safeguards included opposing counsel’s participation
kp.d: The court treated disagreement over whether plaintiffs had consented to predictive coding as immaterial because the protocol incorporated reliability standards, quality assurance and plaintiffs’ participation. Plaintiffs’ counsel could supply keywords and review documents and issue coding before production, with disputed relevance questions referred to the magistrate judge.
qs: Nevertheless, the confusion is immaterial because the ESI protocol contains standards for measuring the reliability of the process and the protocol builds in levels of participation by Plaintiffs.
It provides that the search methods will be carefully crafted and tested for quality assurance, with Plaintiffs participating in their implementation.
For example, Plaintiffs’ counsel may provide keywords and review the documents and the issue coding before the production is made.

kp.k: Reliability objections remained premature rather than empirically disproved
kp.d: Plaintiffs argued that the proposed method lacked generally accepted reliability standards, violated procedural and evidence rules, and had been approved on an insufficient record without a formal evidentiary hearing. The court characterized unreliability claims as premature and speculative at this stage, rather than reporting measured accuracy or a validated sample size. It adopted Peck’s analysis of Rule 26(g) and Federal Rule of Evidence 702 by reference.
qs: Plaintiffs’ arguments concerning the reliability of the method are also premature.
It is difficult to ascertain that the predictive software is less reliable than the traditional keyword search.
The Court adopts Judge Peck’s analysis of Rule 26(g) and Fed. R. Evidence 702 for similar reasons provided in his written opinion.

kp.k: Predictive coding approval remained revisable as discovery progressed
kp.d: The court preserved opportunities to reconsider the method if relevant documents were missing, the software proved flawed or the sample size was inadequate. It acknowledged that MSLGroup held most documentary evidence and plaintiffs had few documents themselves. A later evidentiary hearing remained possible if reliability problems and disagreements persisted, making approval conditional on continuing judicial oversight rather than final acceptance of the tool’s effectiveness.
qs: At this stage, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the use of the predictive coding software will deny Plaintiffs access to liberal discovery.

Judge Peck has ruled that if the predictive coding software is flawed or if Plaintiffs are not receiving the types of documents that should be produced, the parties are allowed to reconsider their methods and raise their concerns with the Magistrate Judge.

If the method provided in the protocol does not work or if the sample size is indeed too small to properly apply the technology, the Court will not preclude Plaintiffs from receiving relevant information, but to call the method unreliable at this stage is speculative.

kp.k: Manual review was costly and subject to human inconsistency
kp.d: The court compared predictive coding with imperfect existing review practices, observing that manual review with keyword searches can be costly and that attorneys differ in responsiveness determinations. It nevertheless recognized manual review as appropriate in some situations. These were qualitative judicial observations, not quantified findings about savings, staffing reductions or accuracy improvements.
qs: There simply is no review tool that guarantees perfection.
Manual review with keyword searches is costly, though appropriate in certain situations.

However, even if all parties here were willing to entertain the notion of manually reviewing the documents, such review is prone to human error and marred with inconsistencies from the various attorneys’ determination of whether a document is responsive.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Andrew L. Carter Jr. permits predictive coding for document review under this case's protocol, rather than establishing its general superiority or reliability.
pts.d: Carter adopts Magistrate Judge Peck's discovery rulings under a highly deferential standard of review. His own reasoning stresses that the protocol provides reliability testing, plaintiffs' participation and opportunities to reconsider the method. He treats objections that predictive coding will impair discovery as premature, not as disproved by measured performance. He also states that manual review with keyword searches is costly and subject to human error and inconsistent responsiveness judgments. These are case-specific claims about computer-assisted discovery, not predictions about generative AI, lawyer displacement or the wider legal market.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The stated basis is review of the litigation record, protocol safeguards and expert participation, not quantitative evidence that predictive coding outperforms other methods.
pts.d: Carter reports reviewing the ESI protocol and parties' submissions and notes that Peck heard experts during the February 8 conference. The protocol includes standards for measuring reliability, quality-assurance testing and plaintiffs' participation. The opinion supplies no measured accuracy, recall, cost savings or comparative benchmark results. Its legal conclusion rests on the record and the Rule 72(a) standard for reviewing nondispositive discovery rulings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Approval applies at the April 2012 discovery stage and remains subject to testing, subsequent production results and judicial reconsideration.
pts.d: The opinion, dated April 25 and filed April 26, 2012, gives no future adoption forecast. Carter finds a definitive adverse reliability judgment speculative at this stage. The parties can raise concerns before final production, revisit the method after production if relevant documents are missing, and potentially receive an evidentiary hearing if reliability problems persist. Approval therefore does not establish that the software or sample size will necessarily prove adequate.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern MSLGroup's document production, plaintiffs' access to relevant evidence, counsel's review responsibilities and judicial oversight.
pts.d: MSLGroup bears most of the documentary production burden. Plaintiffs possess relatively few documents and depend on the production process to obtain relevant information. Their counsel can contribute keywords and review documents and issue coding before production. The court retains oversight and avenues for challenging the method. Carter identifies costs and inconsistencies in manual review but does not quantify savings or predict changes in staffing, fees or legal employment.
